kilauea_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY DAILY UPDATE
kilauea_notices.message: HVO Kilauea ORANGE/WATCH - Multiple overflows and low fountaining occurred from the north vent over the past 24 hours. Kīlauea's summit remains at a high level of pressurization with changes in eruptive activity or location within the summit region possible.
kilauea_notices.detail: See these notices issued October 7: October 7 Hawaiian Volcano Observatory Status Report summarizing recent intrusive activity and implications: https://volcanoes.usgs.gov/hans-public/notice/DOI-USGS-HVO-2026-10-08T01:00:28+00:00 October 7 Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park News Release announcing closures related to recent activity: https://www.nps.gov/havo/learn/news/20261007-nr-trail-closures.htm Summit Observations: Just before 11:30 a.m. HST, the north vent began to vigorously dome fountain for nearly an hour feeding a flow that extended almost a kilometer from the vent. This was the longest and most vigorous dome fountain since September 30. There were two other substantial fountain and overflow episodes around 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. HST that lasted for about 40 minutes and 20 minutes respectively. Interspersed between and following these longer events were about 15 smaller events that lasted only a few minutes and produced flows less than 300 feet (100 meters) long. Sustained fountaining was followed by gas jetting often with sprays of spatter produced during drainback of lava within the vents. The last of these overflow events occurred around 9:30 p.m. HST and only glow with minor gas jetting and spatter were observed from the vents since then. Summit tiltmeters showed slight tilt increases over the past 24 hours including at the Uēkahuna tiltmeter (UWD). In the past 24 hours, there were 20 shallow earthquakes located across the summit region of Kīlauea, predominantly in the south caldera region. GPS stations on opposite sides of Halemaʻumaʻu (CRIM and UWEV) show a small increase in length since the end of September. Updated interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) interferograms following the dike intrusion on September 30-October 1, show the intrusion has been slightly contracting since the evening of October 2. Minor intrusion-related motion was observed along many faults and cracks formed during the 2018 caldera collapse. There are no signs of significant deformation outside the caldera, including the south caldera region. During inter-episode pauses, the sulfur dioxide (SO2) emission rate from the summit typically varies between 1,000 and 5,000 tonnes per day. Plumes of volcanic gas are visible from the vents in day-time webcam views. Winds are currently forecast from the east southeast then changing to from the east this evening. Rift Zone Observations: Rates of seismicity and ground deformation remain low in the East Rift Zone and Southwest Rift Zone. SO2 emissions from the East Rift Zone remain below the detection limit. No significant ground deformation was recorded in either rift zone. Analysis: Kīlauea had been erupting episodically between December 23, 2024, and August 25, 2026, from two vents (north and south) in Halema‘uma‘u at the summit. Lava fountaining episodes generally lasted for less than 12 hours and were separated by pauses of two or more weeks. Irregular patterns of ground deformation at Kīlauea summit since the most recent lava fountaining episode, number 54 on August 25, 2026, prevent forecast modeling for when the next fountaining episode can occur. Ground deformation patterns indicate the magma chamber beneath Halemaʻumaʻu is pressurized beyond the level typically seen before recent fountaining events. This pattern was disrupted by the dike intrusion on September 30-October 1 and since then summit tilt has increased slowly with interspersed periods of decreased or flat tilt. The vigorous overflows yesterday indicates that magma remains very near the surface in the established vent complex and continues to be able to generate smaller fountains. It is possible that another fountaining episode from the north-south vent complex could occur; however, intrusive activity underneath Kaluapele is also possible, or magma could exploit existing weak crack systems in the summit region to erupt passively (with little or no seismicity or deformation). mauna_loa_notices.title: HAWAIIAN VOLCANO OBSERVATORY MONTHLY UPDATE
mauna_loa_notices.message: HVO Mauna Loa GREEN/NORMAL - Mauna Loa earthquake counts decreased in September compared to August, and minor inflation continues.
mauna_loa_notices.detail: Mauna Loa had a decrease in seismic activity compared to the previous month; a total of 53 earthquakes were detected in Mauna Loa's summit region during the September reporting period, after 87 in August. Most earthquakes occurred deep beneath the upper Southwest Rift Zone or broadly scattered around the upper flanks. No earthquakes occurred directly beneath Mokuʻāweoweo. Data from Global Positioning System (GPS) instruments on Mauna Loa showed slight inflation across the summit region in the past month. Oscillations between contraction and inflation patterns during non-eruptive periods are normal, but inflation has been the dominant trend since the 2022 eruption, consistent with magma refilling the summit reservoir system. Gas and temperature data from a station on Mauna Loa's Southwest Rift Zone indicate these values are at background levels, with little change relative to previous months. HVO continues to closely monitor Mauna Loa and will issue another update in one month, or earlier, should conditions change significantly.
